title: The heaviest living thing
teaches: Pando, a grove of aspen that is one plant, what counts as one living thing, the other contenders for biggest, how tall a tree can grow, and why Pando is shrinking

blocks.text: On a mountainside in central Utah, near Fish Lake, grows a grove of quaking aspen covering about 43 hectares, the size of sixty football pitches. It has about 47,000 trunks, white-barked and up to about 25 metres tall, and every one of them is part of a single plant, joined underground by one root system and carrying the same genes. It has a name, Pando, Latin for "I spread", and its weight has been estimated at about 6,000 tonnes, which would make it the heaviest living thing known.[^pando-name]

From the 1960s the forester Burton Barnes mapped aspen clones across the West by eye, from features every trunk in a clone shares: the shape of the leaves, the colour of the bark, and above all the day in autumn when the leaves turn. Look at an aspen-covered hillside in late September and it is a patchwork, one patch gold, the next still green: each patch is one clone. In 2008 a genetic study confirmed that Pando's trunks share one set of genes.

parts.title: How a grove becomes one plant

blocks.text: Aspen seeds are tiny and need bare, wet ground at just the right moment, so in the dry interior West few aspen grow from seed. Instead, an aspen's shallow roots run out sideways for tens of metres and send up new shoots, **suckers**, along the way. Each sucker grows into a trunk with its own crown of leaves, still joined to the roots. When a trunk dies, after about a century, its roots send up suckers in the gap. The trunks come and go; the root system goes on, spreading slowly outward, and can outlive its trunks by thousands of years. Nobody knows how old Pando is: estimates run from several thousand years to tens of thousands.[^pando-age]
A fire that kills every trunk barely touches the roots, which push up suckers in their tens of thousands per hectare the next spring. That is why aspen is one of the first trees back after a burn.

blocks.caption: An aspen clone over 150 years, seen from above. Each dot is a trunk. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, play it, then fence out the deer

blocks.text: For animals the question hardly arises: an elk is one elk. Plants blur it. We can count each aspen trunk as a tree, or the whole grove as one tree, and botanists separate the two meanings. A **clone** is everything grown, without sex, from one original seedling: all its pieces carry the same genes, however many there are.[^ramet] By trunks, Pando is a forest. By clone, it is one plant. Strawberries spreading by runners, grass spreading by underground stems and lesson C4's Red Delicious trees are all clones too. The Red Delicious trees are scattered over orchards worldwide, and spread by grafting instead of by roots.

Pando's record depends on how you count. A honey fungus (*Armillaria ostoyae*) in the Blue Mountains of Oregon spreads its threads under about 900 hectares of forest, twenty times Pando's area, though it is probably lighter. A clone of a seagrass in Shark Bay, Western Australia, covers about 200 square kilometres of sea floor. By single trunk, the giant sequoia called General Sherman in California, about 1,500 cubic metres of wood, is the largest tree by volume, and a coast redwood called Hyperion, 116 metres tall, is the tallest.

How tall can a tree grow? In 2004 George Koch and colleagues climbed the tallest redwoods and measured their leaves at different heights. Near the top, water had to be pulled so hard up the xylem (lesson 6) that the leaves were small and thick, with little room inside for carbon dioxide to reach the cells, and they grew far more slowly than leaves lower down. They estimated that no redwood could grow much past 122 to 130 metres, however long it lived.

Much of Pando has few young trunks. Its trunks are old, and as they die, the suckers that should replace them are bitten off, or browsed, by mule deer and elk, which have few predators there now, and by cattle grazing the forest. Studies led by Paul Rogers of Utah State University found that where parts of the grove had been fenced, suckers grew up thickly; outside the fences, few lived past a deer's reach. More of Pando has been fenced since. Ecology's lesson on why the world is green shows the same pattern elsewhere: what eats the young plants, and what in turn eats the plant-eaters, decides what grows across a valley or hillside.

blocks.caption: Five questions on giant plants
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why is Pando counted as one plant?
choices: All its trunks grow from one root system and share one set of genes
Its trunks were all planted at once
It is surrounded by a fence
items.why: Every trunk is a sucker from the same roots, grown from one original seedling.

items.ask: How can you see separate aspen clones on a hillside?
choices: Each clone turns gold in autumn on its own day
Each clone has a different bark colour every year
items.why: Every trunk in a clone shares its genes, so they change colour together, in patches.

choices: Deer, elk and cattle eat the suckers that should replace old trunks
Its roots are dying of old age
It has run out of room to spread
items.why: Where the grove is fenced, suckers grow up thickly. Outside, few survive browsing.

items.ask: What largely limits how tall a redwood can grow?
choices: How hard water must be pulled up to the top leaves
How much light reaches the lower branches
items.why: Koch's group found the top leaves so short of water they could barely grow, setting a limit of about 122 to 130 metres.

items.ask: Which is a clone in the same sense as Pando?
choices: A patch of strawberries spread by runners from one plant
A field of wheat sown from seed
An orchard of apple trees each grown from seed
items.why: Runners, like aspen roots, carry one plant's genes into new pieces of it.

summary: **Pando is one aspen clone of about 47,000 trunks on 43 hectares.** About 6,000 tonnes: probably the heaviest living thing.
**Aspen spreads by suckers from its roots.** Trunks live about a century; the roots can outlive them by thousands of years.
**A clone is everything grown from one fertilised egg.** By trunks Pando is a forest; by clone, one plant.
**Other records count differently.** A honey fungus and a seagrass cover more ground; General Sherman is the biggest single trunk, Hyperion the tallest.
**Redwoods stop near 122 to 130 metres.** Water can't be pulled any higher fast enough (Koch, 2004).
**Pando is shrinking.** Browsing deer, elk and cattle eat its suckers; fenced parts regrow.

pando-name.title: Who named Pando
pando-name.text: Burton Barnes first described the Fish Lake clone in 1975. In 1992 Michael Grant, Jeffry Mitton and Yan Linhart estimated its weight at about 6,000 tonnes from its trunk count and gave it the name Pando.

pando-age.title: Dating a clone with no old wood
pando-age.text: Tree rings only date a single trunk, and Pando's oldest trunks are little more than a century old. Ice cores from nearby Fish Lake show pollen and charcoal going back no more than about 14,000 years, when glaciers last left the basin. A 2024 study led by Rozenn Pineau sequenced somatic mutations across hundreds of Pando's roots and shoots and estimated the clone is between 16,000 and 80,000 years old.

ramet.title: Genets and ramets
ramet.text: Ecologists call the whole genetic individual a *genet* (the clone) and each separate trunk, shoot or crown within it a *ramet* (from the Latin *ramus*, branch). A ramet can live on its own if its root link to the rest of the clone breaks.
